I was nine the last time I walked with my grandfather to his farm. I remember the dew soaking my sandals, and the way he stopped every few steps to greet a tree as if it were an old friend. He had been a night watchman for eleven years, and in all that time nothing had ever happened. Now his heart was hammering so loudly that he was sure whoever was there could hear it. Before the dawn has opened up its arms,
while sleep still holds the village and its farms,
the fisherman pushes out his narrow boat
and listens to the water's every note.
He knows where tilapia hide at noon,
where currents turn, where nets come up in vain;
he knows the moods and secrets of the moon,
and smells, a day before it falls, the rain.
His sons have gone to work in city towers
where no one reads the water or the sky;
they send him money, phones and plastic flowers,
and ask him why he will not say goodbye.
He smiles, and does not answer them at all:
the lagoon has never asked him to be small.

questions.stem: Examine the conflict between Rome and Egypt in Antony and Cleopatra.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Rome represents duty, discipline, politics and public honour (Caesar, Octavia, the triumvirate)
4 marks: Egypt represents pleasure, passion, luxury and private feeling (Cleopatra, the feasts, Alexandria)
4 marks: Antony is torn between the two worlds: his Roman duty draws him away (Fulvia's death, marriage to Octavia), his love draws him back
4 marks: the conflict leads to tragedy: Actium, defeat and the deaths of both lovers, while cold Roman power (Caesar) triumphs
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the opening complaint of Philo, the marriage to Octavia, the return to Egypt, Actium, the final scenes); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: A good answer shows that the play is built on a contrast between Rome, the world of duty, order and power politics embodied by Octavius Caesar, and Egypt, the world of love, pleasure and imagination embodied by Cleopatra. Antony belongs to both: he leaves Egypt when duty calls, marries Octavia for political reasons, but returns to Cleopatra. His divided loyalty explains his poor judgement at Actium and his fall. Caesar's victory shows the triumph of Rome's cold efficiency, but the lovers' deaths give Egypt a final moral and poetic victory.

questions.stem: Discuss the role of Enobarbus in Antony and Cleopatra.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: he is Antony's loyal and frank friend who speaks plainly and often comments on the action like a chorus
4 marks: his description of Cleopatra on the river Cydnus reveals her fascination and explains Antony's attachment
4 marks: he gives sound advice (against Cleopatra's presence at Actium and against fighting at sea) which Antony ignores
4 marks: his desertion and death of grief after Antony's generosity show Antony's decline and nobility and the theme of loyalty
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the barge description, the advice before Actium, the desertion, Antony sending his treasure, his death); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Enobarbus is Antony's blunt, witty companion who sees events clearly and comments on them, often guiding the audience's judgement. He describes Cleopatra's splendour more powerfully than anyone, explaining why Antony cannot leave her. He advises sensibly before Actium, and his warnings prove right. When he finally deserts, Antony's generosity in sending his treasure breaks his heart, and he dies in shame. His story highlights the themes of loyalty and judgement and marks the stages of Antony's fall.

questions.stem: To what extent is Antony responsible for his own downfall in Antony and Cleopatra?
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: his passion for Cleopatra makes him neglect his duties and act against good judgement
4 marks: he insults Caesar by abandoning Octavia and returning to Egypt, provoking war
4 marks: he chooses to fight at sea at Actium against advice and follows Cleopatra's fleeing ships
4 marks: other forces also contribute: Caesar's ambition and efficiency, the desertion of followers, Cleopatra's fleet yielding and the false report of her death
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. Actium, the treatment of Octavia, the Soothsayer's warning, the final battle, Mardian's report); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: A balanced answer argues that Antony is largely responsible: his infatuation leads him to neglect Rome, to treat Octavia badly and to make the disastrous decision to fight at sea and then to flee after Cleopatra. Yet Caesar's cold ambition, the shifting loyalties of his followers, the yielding of the Egyptian fleet and Cleopatra's false message also play their part. Antony is a tragic hero whose own flaw, combined with circumstances, destroys him.

questions.stem: Discuss the theme of prejudice in To Kill a Mockingbird.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: racial prejudice: Tom Robinson is convicted despite clear evidence of his innocence because he is black
4 marks: prejudice against Boo Radley: the town and the children fear him because of rumours, though he is kind
4 marks: class prejudice: attitudes to the Cunninghams and Ewells, and Aunt Alexandra's ideas of "fine folks"
4 marks: Atticus and others (Miss Maudie, Heck Tate) challenge prejudice; Scout learns to see from other people's point of view
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the trial, the lynch mob scene, the gifts in the tree, Walter Cunningham at lunch, the ending on the Radley porch); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: The novel shows prejudice in many forms. Racial prejudice leads the jury to convict Tom Robinson although Atticus proves that Mayella's injuries were caused by a left-handed man. The town's fear of Boo Radley is based on gossip, yet Boo protects the children. Class snobbery appears in attitudes to the Cunninghams and in Aunt Alexandra's views. Atticus teaches his children to stand in other people's shoes, and Scout's final view from the Radley porch shows that she has learnt to overcome prejudice.

questions.stem: Discuss Atticus Finch as a father and as a lawyer in To Kill a Mockingbird.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: as a father he is patient, fair and treats his children as thinking individuals
4 marks: he teaches by example: courage (Mrs Dubose), empathy (standing in another's shoes), honesty
4 marks: as a lawyer he defends Tom Robinson with skill and integrity despite threats and certain defeat
4 marks: he faces the lynch mob, endures insults from Bob Ewell and the town, and remains calm and principled
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the mad dog scene, Mrs Dubose, the jail scene, the trial, his response to Ewell spitting on him); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Atticus is a model father: he answers his children's questions honestly, treats them with respect and teaches them courage and empathy through his own conduct. As a lawyer he accepts Tom Robinson's case knowing he will lose, defends him skilfully by exposing the Ewells' lies, and sits guard at the jail. His calm response to Bob Ewell's insults shows his moral strength. He is the moral centre of the novel.

questions.stem: What is the significance of Boo Radley in To Kill a Mockingbird?
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: at first he is a figure of mystery and fear for the children, built on rumours
4 marks: his secret gifts in the tree and the blanket during the fire show his kindness and his wish for contact
4 marks: he saves Jem and Scout from Bob Ewell, proving the rumours wrong
4 marks: he is one of the "mockingbirds": an innocent who must be protected, which is why Heck Tate shields him
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the games about Boo, the knot-hole gifts, the fire, the Halloween attack, Scout on the Radley porch); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Boo Radley begins as the children's monster, a creature of town gossip. Gradually his gifts in the oak tree, the blanket around Scout during the fire and the mended trousers reveal a gentle, lonely man. His rescue of the children shows how wrong prejudice is. Heck Tate and Atticus agree to protect him, since exposing him would be like killing a mockingbird. Through Boo, Scout learns to understand others.

questions.stem: Discuss Ananse as a trickster in The Marriage of Anansewa.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: he is poor but clever and decides to use his daughter to obtain wealth
4 marks: he deceives four chiefs at once, collecting gifts from all of them
4 marks: when trapped, he invents the "death" of Anansewa and manages events to his advantage
4 marks: he is amusing and resourceful but his scheme exposes greed and the commercialisation of marriage; he is also a loving father who wants a good future for his daughter
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the photographs and letters to the chiefs, the gifts, the arrival of messengers, the staged death, the final marriage); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Ananse, like the spider of Akan tales, lives by his wits. Being poor, he sends his daughter's photograph to four chiefs and accepts gifts from each. When all of them plan to come, he stages Anansewa's death and then uses the chiefs' responses to identify the true lover, Chief-Who-Is-Chief. He is comic and ingenious, but his scheme also satirises greed and the treatment of marriage as a business, though he does want security for his daughter.

questions.stem: Examine the role of the Storyteller in The Marriage of Anansewa.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: he links the scenes and narrates events, as in traditional Ananse storytelling
4 marks: he comments on the characters and action and sometimes judges Ananse
4 marks: he involves the audience directly, making them participants rather than spectators
4 marks: he is central to Sutherland's Anansegoro form, which adapts oral storytelling (with songs) to the stage
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. his introductions, his comments on Ananse's scheme, the songs, his addresses to the audience); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: The Storyteller acts as narrator and link between the play and its audience. He introduces and connects episodes, comments on Ananse's behaviour and invites the audience to respond, so that the performance resembles a traditional storytelling session. Through him Sutherland creates the Anansegoro, a modern African theatre form rooted in oral tradition.

questions.stem: Discuss the role of the Inspector in An Inspector Calls.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: he reveals step by step how each member of the family contributed to Eva Smith's death
4 marks: he acts as Priestley's voice for social responsibility against Mr Birling's selfish capitalism
4 marks: he controls the pace and tension of the play, questioning one character at a time
4 marks: his mysterious identity (Goole) and the final telephone call suggest he is a moral or supernatural force that will return
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the photograph, the questioning of each character, his final speech about responsibility, the ending); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Inspector Goole drives the action: he questions each Birling and Gerald in turn, showing how each helped to destroy Eva Smith. He speaks for Priestley's belief that we are all responsible for one another, opposing Birling's view that a man should look after himself. He controls the drama's tension, and his uncertain identity, together with the final phone call, suggests that he is a moral force whose warning cannot be escaped.

questions.stem: Compare the reactions of the older and younger generations of the Birling family to the Inspector's visit.
questions.markingGuide:

4 marks: they are relieved when they suspect the Inspector was a hoax and return to their old attitudes
4 marks: Sheila and Eric accept their guilt and are changed by what they learn
4 marks: the contrast expresses Priestley's hope that the young can build a more caring society
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. Birling's fear of losing his knighthood, Mrs Birling's denial, Sheila's warning to Gerald and her parents, Eric's outburst, the ending); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Mr and Mrs Birling remain arrogant and self-protective: they deny any blame and, once they suspect a hoax, celebrate as if nothing had happened. Sheila and Eric, however, are shaken and accept that they helped to destroy Eva; they insist that the lesson stands whether or not the Inspector was real. Priestley uses the contrast to show his hope in the younger generation.

questions.topic: A Man for All Seasons (Robert Bolt)
questions.stem: Discuss Sir Thomas More as a man of conscience in A Man for All Seasons.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: he refuses to approve the King's divorce and remarriage or to swear the oath because it is against his conscience
4 marks: he uses the law and silence skilfully to protect himself without lying
4 marks: he gives up office, wealth and comfort and endures imprisonment rather than betray himself
4 marks: he remains calm, gentle and witty, and dies rather than compromise, in contrast with Rich and Cromwell
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. his resignation as Lord Chancellor, his refusal of the oath, the Tower scenes with his family, the trial and Rich's perjury, the execution); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: More is a man who will not act against his conscience. He resigns as Lord Chancellor and keeps silent about the King's marriage, relying on the law to protect him. He suffers loss of property and imprisonment and resists the pleas of his family. Only Rich's perjury secures his conviction. His calm, witty dignity, contrasted with the ambition of Rich and Cromwell, makes him a hero of integrity.

questions.topic: A Man for All Seasons (Robert Bolt)
questions.stem: Trace the rise of Richard Rich in A Man for All Seasons and show what it reveals about the theme of corruption.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Rich begins as a poor, ambitious young man seeking a post; More advises him to be a teacher
4 marks: he accepts a silver cup from More and is soon drawn into Cromwell's service, giving information
4 marks: he commits perjury at More's trial to secure More's conviction
4 marks: his reward, the post of Attorney-General for Wales, shows how power corrupts and how cheaply conscience can be sold
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the opening scene, the silver cup, the scene with Cromwell, the trial); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Rich starts as a needy scholar whom More advises to become a teacher. Unable to resist ambition, he accepts More's silver cup and then sells information to Cromwell. At the trial he lies under oath that More denied the King's title. He is rewarded with the post of Attorney-General for Wales. His rise shows how ambition leads, step by step, to the betrayal of truth and friendship.

questions.stem: Discuss the theme of the loss of innocence in Gabriel Okara's "Once Upon a Time".
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: the father recalls a past when people were sincere, laughing with their hearts and eyes
4 marks: now people are hypocritical; their smiles and handshakes hide coldness and selfishness
4 marks: the father admits that he too has learned to wear different faces and say what he does not mean
4 marks: he wants to relearn from his son, the symbol of innocence, how to laugh sincerely
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the contrast of past and present, the images of faces and handshakes, the mirror, the appeal to the son); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: The poem contrasts a past of sincerity with a present of hypocrisy. The father says people now laugh only with their teeth and shake hands without warmth. He confesses that he has adopted many false faces for different occasions and that his own laugh frightens him. He asks his son to teach him how to laugh again, seeing in the child the innocence that adults have lost.

questions.stem: Discuss the poet's use of repetition and irony in Niyi Osundare's "Not My Business".
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: the refrain, in which the speaker says it is not his business so long as his food is safe, is repeated after each incident
4 marks: the repetition emphasises his growing selfishness and indifference
4 marks: the incidents (Akanni beaten and taken, Danladi taken at night, Chinwe losing her job) build a picture of oppression
4 marks: irony: at the end the jeep waits at his own door, showing that indifference does not protect anyone
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the three victims, the refrain, the final stanza); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Osundare repeats the speaker's selfish refrain after each act of oppression: the brutal arrest of Akanni, the night raid on Danladi and Chinwe's sudden dismissal. The repetition stresses his indifference. The poem ends with the jeep waiting for him, an ironic reversal that shows that those who ignore injustice to others will themselves become victims.

questions.stem: Examine the use of imagery in Lord Byron's "She Walks in Beauty".
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: the opening simile compares the woman to a cloudless, starry night
4 marks: imagery of light and darkness is balanced throughout to suggest harmony
4 marks: physical features (hair, face, cheek, brow) are described in gentle, soft images
4 marks: outer beauty is linked to inner goodness: a peaceful mind and an innocent heart
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the night simile, the balance of dark and bright, the final stanza's reference to her mind and heart); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Byron compares the woman to a clear starry night, combining darkness and light. This balance continues through the poem, where her dark hair and bright face form a perfect harmony. The gentle imagery of her features leads to the final idea that her beauty reflects a calm mind and an innocent heart.

questions.stem: Discuss "The Nun's Priest's Tale" as a moral fable.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: it is a beast fable in which animals (Chauntecleer, Pertelote, the fox) behave like humans
4 marks: it warns against pride and vanity: Chauntecleer is flattered into closing his eyes
4 marks: it warns against flattery: the fox's praise leads to capture
4 marks: the escape, when Chauntecleer tricks the fox into speaking, teaches that one should be watchful and not speak carelessly; it is told in a mock-heroic style
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the dream and the debate with Pertelote, the fox's flattery, the chase, the escape); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: The tale is a fable in which a proud cock, his wife and a cunning fox behave like people. Chauntecleer ignores his own dream and is flattered by the fox into singing with his eyes shut. During the chase he tricks the fox into opening his mouth to boast and escapes. Both learn lessons: the cock not to be fooled by flattery and the fox not to speak when he should keep quiet. The mock-heroic treatment adds humour.

questions.stem: Discuss the relationship between the speaker and his ancestors in Seamus Heaney's "Digging".
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: the speaker watches his father digging in the garden and remembers him digging potatoes in his prime
4 marks: he admires the skill and strength of his father and grandfather (the grandfather cutting turf)
4 marks: he feels a sense of difference, since he has no spade to follow them
4 marks: he resolves to continue the family tradition in his own way by "digging" with his pen
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the opening image of the pen, the father in the flowerbeds and potato drills, the grandfather on the bog, the closing resolution); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: The speaker, sitting with his pen, hears his father digging and recalls him and the grandfather at work, admiring their skill. He feels separated from them because he will not use a spade, but he resolves to dig with his pen, uncovering memories through writing. The poem thus moves from admiration and distance to a sense of continuity.

questions.stem: Examine the theme of resilience in Maya Angelou's "Still I Rise".
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: the speaker addresses those who oppress and belittle her and declares she will rise above them
4 marks: images of natural forces (dust, air, tides, moons and suns) suggest her rising is natural and unstoppable
4 marks: images of wealth (oil wells, gold mines, diamonds) express confidence and self-worth
4 marks: she rises out of a painful history of oppression, carrying the hopes of her ancestors; the repeated refrain reinforces her determination
5 marks: Relevant illustration from the text (e.g. the questions to the oppressor, the images of nature and wealth, the reference to history, the refrain); no quotation needed but accurate reference to events and characters
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: The speaker challenges those who would put her down and repeatedly declares that she will rise. She uses images of nature to show that her rising is as certain as the tides, and images of wealth to show her confidence. She refers to a history of oppression and presents herself as the hope of her ancestors. The insistent refrain makes the poem a song of triumph and resilience.

questions.stem:
Read the poem below carefully and answer the questions.

MARKET WOMAN

Before the cock has cleared its throat
she is already on the road,
a mountain of tomatoes on her head,
her baby a warm parcel on her back.

All day she sings her prices
to the deaf ears of the sun;
she argues, laughs, forgives,
counts naira notes as soft as old cloth.

At dusk she walks home lighter,
the mountain gone, the parcel asleep,
and in her fist, tight as a promise,
the school fees of a child.

(a) What is the subject matter of the poem? [5 marks]
(b) Identify and comment on two figures of speech in the poem. [8 marks]
(c) Describe the mood of the last stanza. [4 marks]
(d) What is the poet's attitude to the market woman? [4 marks]
(e) Comment on the structure of the poem. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) the hard daily life of a market woman who works from before dawn to dusk to pay for her child's education
8 marks: (b) any two, 4 marks each (identification 1, quotation from the poem 1, comment 2): metaphor "a mountain of tomatoes" (hyperbole of the load), metaphor "her baby a warm parcel", personification "the cock has cleared its throat" / "the deaf ears of the sun", simile "as soft as old cloth" / "tight as a promise"
4 marks: (c) quiet satisfaction / fulfilment and hope: her load is gone, the baby sleeps and she has earned the school fees
4 marks: (d) admiration, respect and sympathy for her hard work, patience and sacrifice
4 marks: (e) three four-line stanzas in free verse, arranged in time order: dawn, day, dusk
questions.explanation: The poem (written for this item) presents a market woman's day from before dawn to dusk. Figures include the metaphor of the tomatoes as a mountain (also exaggeration), the baby as a 'warm parcel', the personified sun with 'deaf ears' and the simile 'tight as a promise'. The final stanza is calm and fulfilled, since her sacrifice has earned her child's school fees. The poet admires her endurance. The poem's three unrhymed quatrains follow the stages of her day.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between tragedy and comedy as dramatic forms. [10 marks]
(b) Explain, with an original example of each, the following figures of speech: (i) oxymoron (ii) litotes (iii) apostrophe (iv) synecdoche (v) pathetic fallacy. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) tragedy: serious subject, a hero of stature brought down by a flaw or fate, ends in suffering or death, arouses pity and fear (catharsis) (5); comedy: lighter subject, ordinary characters, humour and complications resolved happily, often in marriage or reconciliation, aims to amuse and correct (5)
3 marks: (b)(i) oxymoron: two contradictory words placed together, e.g. "a cheerful funeral" (definition 2, example 1)
3 marks: (b)(ii) litotes: understatement by denying the opposite, e.g. "She is no fool" (definition 2, example 1)
3 marks: (b)(iii) apostrophe: direct address to an absent person, the dead or an abstraction, e.g. "O Freedom, when will you come?" (definition 2, example 1)
3 marks: (b)(iv) synecdoche: a part stands for the whole or the whole for a part, e.g. "We need more hands on the farm" (definition 2, example 1)
3 marks: (b)(v) pathetic fallacy: attributing human feelings to nature, often reflecting the mood, e.g. "The clouds frowned on the mourners" (definition 2, example 1)
questions.explanation: Tragedy deals seriously with the fall of a significant hero through a flaw or fate and ends in catastrophe, producing pity and fear; comedy treats life lightly, uses humour and confusion and ends happily. Oxymoron joins contradictory terms; litotes understates by negating the opposite; apostrophe addresses the absent or abstract; synecdoche uses part for whole; pathetic fallacy gives nature human feelings.
